clue.text: Back of glass lamp is flimsy (6)

indicators.note: The back of a word is its final letter, so only the rear end of the word that follows is wanted.

blocks.note: the closing letter of 'glass', taken because only its rear is asked for
a lamp is a light, the ordinary word for the thing on the table

annotation.surface: The rear of a glass lamp turns out to be poorly made.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back of' looks like part of the picture — the rear of the lamp — and it is an instruction about letters instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Slight means thin and insubstantial, as a slight partition or a slight frame is, which is what calling something flimsy says of it.

blocks.note: sp is the standard short form of special, as chalked on a menu board
a ring is a syndicate of people running something crooked — a drugs ring, a betting ring

annotation.surface: Somebody abruptly sets up a few special consortia.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Special' looks like an adjective attached to the syndicates beside it, and it is a two-letter abbreviation standing entirely on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: To spring is to move all at once and without warning, so a thing that springs starts suddenly rather than merely beginning.

indicators.note: A shroud wraps right round whatever it covers, so the words after it are concealing what is wanted inside themselves.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters running out of the middle of the first word and into the second

annotation.surface: Nightfall coming down over Berlin, with a river somewhere in the gloom.
annotation.walkthrough: Berlin and dusk together paint a German evening, and the river hidden in them runs through Pakistan — the picture points at the wrong continent entirely.
annotation.definitionFit: The Indus is the great river of Pakistan, so 'river' defines it by class: one named instance of the thing.

indicators.note: Anything done carelessly is done without attention to where things end up, so these letters land out of their proper places.

blocks.note: nine letters of raw material, the verb and its object run together

annotation.surface: Someone who stashed their possessions sloppily, looking back on it later.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hid' invites you to hunt for something buried inside the clue, which is what a concealed answer would ask for; the two words are raw material to be shuffled.
annotation.definitionFit: Retrospect is the backward look taken at events once they are over, the same understanding-after-the-fact that hindsight names.

indicators.note: What is broadcast goes out over the air and arrives as sound, so what follows is wanted for the noise it makes rather than the way it is written.

blocks.note: the flip side of a single carried the song nobody bought the record for, and those two syllables said aloud can be written a second way

annotation.surface: An instruction to the radio station to play the obscure old songs too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is a favourite anagram indicator and here it means the other thing, said aloud. A seven-inch single had its hit on one face and a filler on the other.
annotation.definitionFit: 'As well' means in addition, and besides carries that same additive sense — 'besides, there's the cost' — rather than its other meaning of alongside.

blocks.note: a bitter wind is a freezing one, the word English keeps for cold that hurts
n is the compass abbreviation for north, as printed on any map

annotation.surface: A bird you would only come across in the icy far north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Found in' looks like a container instruction, one thing sitting inside another, and it is only joinery saying the definition equals what comes next.
annotation.definitionFit: A bittern is a heron of the reedbeds, famous for its foghorn boom, so 'bird' defines it by class.

clue.text: Vowel sound endings in Thomas’ poetic triumph wow Swansea (5)

indicators.note: An ending is the letter a word finishes on, and 'in' points at the list following, so every word there gives up its last one.

blocks.note: the closing letter of the poet's name
the closing letter of 'poetic'
the closing letter of 'triumph'
the closing letter of 'wow', which is the letter it opens with as well
the closing letter of the Welsh city where Dylan Thomas was born and grew up

annotation.surface: A poetic triumph of Thomas's leaving his home town delighted.
annotation.walkthrough: Dylan Thomas came from Swansea, which is what holds the surface together. A schwa is the flat unstressed uh at the end of 'sofa', the commonest vowel in English speech.
annotation.definitionFit: A schwa is the neutral unstressed vowel written ə, so it is a vowel sound rather than any vowel letter.

indicators.note: 'Before' fixes the running order: what it follows is placed in front of what comes after it.

blocks.note: a DI is a detective inspector in a British force, and the plural of that rank adds the s
the formal accusation read out when somebody is booked is a charge

annotation.surface: Setting some policemen at liberty before anyone gets round to accusing them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Free' reads as an adjective describing those officers, which is the wrong part of speech: the word wanted is the verb, what a court does to a defendant.
annotation.definitionFit: To discharge somebody is to release them from custody or from a duty, which is 'free' used as a verb: to set at liberty.

indicators.note: What a thing absorbs is taken into it and kept there, so the letter named next vanishes inside the word before it.

blocks.note: the open summer shoe held on by straps
c is the letter on the cold tap and the weather map's short form

annotation.surface: A sandal soaking up the cold wet dirt of a puddle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mud' is the slung sort, the stuff a reputation gets dragged through, rather than anything on the path — which is where the shoe is trying to send you.
annotation.definitionFit: Mud in the sense of damaging talk — mud-slinging, a name dragged through it — is the same currency as a scandal, so the two swap.

blocks.note: s is the size printed on a clothing label
an ample supply is more than enough, a plain synonym

annotation.surface: A helping quite big enough for anybody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Small enough' looks like a single measurement of the portion, and the setter has split it down the middle into two unrelated jobs.
annotation.definitionFit: A sample is the small portion taken to stand for the whole — the spoonful at the deli counter — so 'portion' is its plain sense.

clue.text: No longer needed and turned around (9)

indicators.note: Sending something around moves it out of its place and back by another route, so these letters arrive in a fresh order.

blocks.note: nine letters of raw material, the little conjunction counted in

annotation.surface: Something nobody wants any more, and spun about for good measure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like the joint between the two halves of the clue, and it is material itself — leave it out and the letter count comes up three short.
annotation.definitionFit: A redundant worker or part is one there is no further need for, so 'no longer needed' is the phrase the workplace uses for it.

blocks.note: a crush is a dense pack of people, and a host is that same multitude
the clue's own indefinite article, taken as the single letter it already is

annotation.surface: Somebody stamping a plant flat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crush' reads as the verb, stamp it flat, and the noun is wanted: the crowd sense, as in a crush at the doors.
annotation.definitionFit: A hosta is the broad-leaved shade plant of countless gardens, so 'plant' names it by class.

clue.text: Loch contains third of otters’ dens (5)

indicators.note: What contains something has it inside itself, so the letter named next goes within the word before it.
'Third of' counts three letters into the word that follows and takes only the one it lands on.

blocks.note: the most famous loch in Scotland, the one with the monster
counting three letters in from the start of the word lands on this one

annotation.surface: A loch holding a third of the local otters' homes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Contains third of' reads as a fraction, a third of all the dens, and it is really two separate instructions about letters standing side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: Nests are the homes animals build for themselves and their young, which is what dens are — the same lair sense, and plural to match.

clue.text: E Shepard working over introduction to Winnie-the-Pooh laid initial coat of paint? (3-6)

indicators.note: To give something a working over is to knock it thoroughly out of shape, which is what becomes of the order of these letters.
An introduction comes at the very front, so only the opening letter of the name that follows is taken.

blocks.note: eight letters of raw material: E. H. Shepard drew the original illustrations for A. A. Milne's bear
the opening letter of the bear's name, joining the material to be shuffled

annotation.surface: Shepard labouring over the opening of Winnie-the-Pooh, having put down a first coat of paint.
annotation.walkthrough: A wash is a thin coat of paint brushed on before the proper one, which is the sense the definition turns on, and the hyphen falls after three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Something pre-washed has had that preliminary wash of colour laid on first, and the question mark flags how far the setter is stretching the everyday word.

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: it is a mass noun naming the pebbles of a beach collectively, which is why a plural gloss is fair.

indicators.note: What holds a thing keeps it inside itself, so the letter named next sits within the word before it.

blocks.note: a single is one of anything — one room, one ticket, one record
h is the letter on the hot tap

annotation.surface: Someone carrying a handful of warm stones.
annotation.walkthrough: Shingle is the coarse pebble covering of a beach, the stuff that crunches underfoot at Brighton, and 'One' is not the numeral but the word for a solitary thing.
annotation.definitionFit: Shingle is the mass of water-worn stones that makes up such a beach, so 'pebbles' names exactly what it consists of.

clue.text: Cossie designed by the French with two sides the same (9)

indicators.note: Something designed has been deliberately laid out afresh, so these letters are set down in an order somebody else chose.

blocks.note: six letters of raw material; a cossie is what British beachgoers call a swimming costume
'the' in French, in the form used before a plural noun

annotation.surface: A swimsuit run up by French designers, cut identically on both sides.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the sentence mentions triangles: it reads as a fashion credit, and the French definite article is a piece of crossword vocabulary worth keeping by you.
annotation.definitionFit: An isosceles triangle is the one whose two sides are of equal length, so the phrase gives its defining property rather than a synonym.

indicators.note: 'Part of' says what is wanted is a stretch already sitting inside the words that follow, in the order they are given.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters beginning four into the first word and stepping over the apostrophe into the second

annotation.surface: The first instalment of a journalist's three-book series.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opening' reads as the start of that trilogy and means an aperture instead. The apostrophe is stepped straight over, which is where the run of letters usually gets lost.
annotation.definitionFit: A nostril is one of the two openings of the nose, so 'opening' defines it by what it is: a hole letting something through.

indicators.note: What restrains a thing holds it in and stops it getting out, so the piece named next is trapped inside the word before it.

blocks.note: a stent is the little tube a surgeon leaves in an artery to hold it open
a plain band of metal worn on a finger

annotation.surface: A splint fitted for the time being, stopping a bandage from slipping.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tight' is the strict sense — tight rules, tight security — not anything physically taut, and 'band' is the metal kind rather than the musical one.
annotation.definitionFit: Stringent rules are tightly drawn and rigidly enforced, which is 'tight' in its figurative sense: a tight ship, tight controls.

clue.text: Chicken roll includes last slice of tomato (7)

indicators.note: What includes something has it in among its own parts, so the letter named next goes inside the word before it.
A slice off the end of a word is one letter, and 'last' says take the one at the back.

blocks.note: a roll of names, the list read out at a meeting, is a roster
the closing letter of the word

annotation.surface: A chicken roll made up with the end slice of a tomato in it.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is food — chicken, roll, tomato — and not one of them is doing food work: the bird is alive and the roll is a list of names.
annotation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male chicken, the farmyard cock, so 'chicken' names it by species: one member of the kind.

blocks.note: re heads a memo to mean 'concerning', and crosswords lean on it constantly
the dull pains left by a cold or a long walk are aches

annotation.surface: A body stretching itself out to ease a set of nagging pains.
annotation.walkthrough: RE is the crossword's workhorse for 'concerning', the word at the head of a memo, and it opens more answers than any other pair of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To reach is to stretch a hand out towards something, so the plural verb matches the definition's own stretching sense.

blocks.note: a steak served underdone is a rare one
a bit is a piece of something — a bit of cake, a bit of string

annotation.surface: An undercooked scrap of something found in a toasted cheese sandwich.
annotation.walkthrough: Welsh rarebit is seasoned melted cheese poured over toast, a British supper dish, and 'in' is doing nothing but joining the clue's two halves.
annotation.definitionFit: Rarebit is that dish of melted cheese on toast, still on pub menus as Welsh rarebit, which is what 'cheese toastie' describes in modern words.

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel, the crossword's usual scruffy dog
rent is the past tense of rend: cloth that was torn was rent

annotation.surface: A dog ripping its way into a river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tore into' reads as one phrase, the dog laying about something, and 'into' is only the joint between the wordplay and the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A current is the body of water moving steadily in one direction through a river or a sea, so 'moving water' says what it is.

indicators.note: To catch what somebody says is to hear it, so the word before is wanted for its sound — a loose signal, and the only pointer to sound the clue offers.

blocks.note: somebody who trades is a seller, and those two syllables said aloud can be written another way
y is the algebra teacher's unknown quantity, alongside x and z

annotation.surface: A market trader stopped by the police with an unidentified vegetable on him.
annotation.walkthrough: The unknown vegetable is a policeman's problem in the surface and a single letter in the wordplay, tacked onto the end of a spoken 'seller'.
annotation.definitionFit: Celery is the pale ribbed stalk eaten raw with cheese or chopped into a soup base, so 'vegetable' names it by class.

clue.text: Express hesitation in outline for bank (7)

indicators.note: 'In' is the plainest of the insertion instructions: the letters just named are dropped inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: the noise a speaker makes while groping for the next word, written down as two letters
to outline a shape on paper is to trace it

annotation.surface: Someone voicing their doubts about a sketch drawn up for a bank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank' sends everybody to money and the sense wanted is a level bank of earth cut into a slope — the same word gardeners and hillside farmers use.
annotation.definitionFit: A terrace is a flat bank of ground raised or cut out of a hillside, so 'bank' means the ridge of earth and nothing financial.

indicators.note: A thing run badly is not kept in proper order, so the letters beside it come out in disarray.

blocks.note: nine letters of raw material, the verb and the building together

annotation.surface: A family that managed its castle poorly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Family' is doing adjective work — the family home, the family silver — which is how it sits at the front looking like the subject of the sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Ancestral means belonging to one's forebears, and 'family' does the same adjectival job: the family seat is the ancestral seat.

indicators.note: 'Finally' asks for what comes at the very end, so only the closing letter of the next word is taken.

blocks.note: the closing letter of the word
an idle worker is a lazy one, straight synonym

annotation.surface: Sacking somebody bone-idle at long last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Creep' reads as the noun a sacked colleague might be called, and the verb is wanted: to move sideways and furtively along a wall.
annotation.definitionFit: To sidle is to edge along sideways hoping not to be noticed, which is 'creep' in its verb sense of moving unseen.

blocks.note: N is the dictionary's short form for Norse, the label stamped on Old Norse word origins
an ewer is the wide-lipped jug that stood beside a washbasin

annotation.surface: A Viking pitcher dug up later than the rest of the hoard.
annotation.walkthrough: EWER is one of those words crosswords keep in circulation long after the object left the house, and it turns up wherever a clue says jug or pitcher.
annotation.definitionFit: Newer means of a later date, so between two finds the newer one is whichever came to light more recently.

clue.text: Which person starts to organise party cheer? (5)

indicators.note: A word's start is its first letter, and the plural reading takes one from the front of each word that follows.

blocks.note: the question word that asks exactly that
the opening letter of each of the two words, taken in order

annotation.surface: Somebody asking who is going to start getting the party cheer organised.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole sentence reads as one question about who will get things going, and only the final word is the definition — everything before it is instructions.
annotation.definitionFit: A whoop is the loud cry of delight let out at good news, so 'cheer' means a shout of approval rather than comfort or good spirits.

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the words beside it are wanted for the way they sound.

blocks.note: the cargo space below a ship's deck is its hold, and that syllable said aloud can be spelt a second way

annotation.surface: News coming in that part of a ship has been deliberately sunk.
annotation.walkthrough: To scuttle a vessel is to sink it on purpose by breaching the hull, which is the state the definition is describing rather than any hurried movement.
annotation.definitionFit: A scuttled ship has had its hull opened up to let the sea in, so it has been holed, and both words sit in the past tense.

clue.text: Ban Charlie dancing alone in the city (9)

indicators.note: Dancers keep changing places with one another, so the letters told to dance finish somewhere other than where they started.

blocks.note: to bar somebody from a place is to ban them
Charlie is C in the radio alphabet, alongside Alpha and Bravo
five letters of raw material, shuffled out of their given order

annotation.surface: Charlie barred from the club and dancing by himself somewhere in town.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is one picture of a lone reveller, and the definition is only the last two words; the place meant is Spain's second-largest, on the Mediterranean.
annotation.definitionFit: Barcelona is the Catalan capital on Spain's east coast, so 'the city' defines it by class: one particular example of one.

clue.text: Dodgy extract of forest ceps usually sent back (7)

indicators.note: To extract is to pull something out of what it is sitting in, so the letters wanted are already there in the words that follow.
In an across entry, something sent back is read the other way along the row, from the right-hand end towards the left.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters spanning the three words, read from the right-hand end back towards the left

annotation.surface: A dubious mushroom extract that customers usually send back.
annotation.walkthrough: Ceps are the fat brown wild mushrooms prized in French cooking, and every word of the sentence keeps that food-complaint picture going except the first.
annotation.definitionFit: Something dodgy is not to be trusted, and suspect wiring or a suspect motive is exactly that — the adjective, not the noun for a person.

blocks.note: the verb: to fasten sheets of paper together with a little wire clip
the noun: the basic food a whole diet rests on, rice or maize or bread

annotation.surface: An instruction to lock down the food supplies nobody can do without.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Secure' reads as an adjective describing that food, safely stored away, and the sense wanted is the office verb done with a wire clip.
annotation.definitionFit: To staple is to fasten with such a clip, and a staple is the basic foodstuff a diet depends on, so the two senses share only a spelling.
